{{Short description|Set of integers, the lengths of the sides of a triangle with a 60° angle}}
Similar to a [[Pythagorean triple]], an '''Eisenstein triple''' (named after [[Gotthold Eisenstein]]) is a set of [[integer]]s which are the lengths of the sides of a [[triangle]] where one of the angles is 60 or 120 degrees. The relation of such triangles to the [[Eisenstein integer]]s is analogous to the relation of Pythagorean triples to the [[Gaussian integer]]s.

==Triangles with an angle of 60°==
[[Image:Eisenstein triple.png|thumb|An Eisenstein triple]]
Triangles with an angle of 60° are a special case of the [[Law of Cosines]]:<ref>Gilder, J., Integer-sided triangles with an angle of 60°," Mathematical Gazette 66, December 1982, 261 266</ref><ref>Burn, Bob, "Triangles with a 60° angle and sides of integer length," Mathematical Gazette 87, March 2003, 148–153.</ref><ref>Read, Emrys, "On integer-sided triangles containing angles of 120° or 60°", ''Mathematical Gazette'', 90, July 2006, 299–305.</ref>

:<math>c^2 = a^2 - ab + b^2.</math>

When the lengths of the sides are integers, the values form a set known as an Eisenstein triple.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www2.edc.org/cme/showcase/slides.delaware.2006.pdf |title=Archived copy |access-date=2014-05-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060723174300/http://www2.edc.org/cme/showcase/slides.delaware.2006.pdf |archive-date=2006-07-23 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Examples of Eisenstein triples include:<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.had2know.com/academics/integer-triangles-60-degree-angle.html|title=Integer Triangles with a 60-Degree Angle}}</ref>

==Triangles with an angle of 120°==
[[Image:120-degree-integer-triangle.svg|thumb|Triangle with 120° angle and integer sides]]
A similar special case of the Law of Cosines relates the sides of a triangle with an angle of 120 degrees:

:<math>c^2 = a^2 + ab + b^2.</math>

Examples of such triangles include:<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.had2know.com/academics/integer-triangles-120-degree-angle.html|title = Integer Triangles with a 120-Degree Angle}}</ref>
